# Introduction to Deuteronomy

## Part 1: General Introduction

### Outline of Deuteronomy

1. The author’s introduction of Moses’ speech (1:1–5)
2. Moses’ first speech (1:6–4:40)
3. Cities of refuge selected for the Reubenites, Gadites, and Manassites (4:41–43)
4. The author’s introduction of the Law (4:44-49)
5. Moses’ second speech (5:1–26:19)
6. Moses’ third speech (27:1–28:68)
7. The author’s summary (29:1)
8. The covenant renewed (29:2–30:20)
9. Last words of Moses, the Song of Moses, and his death (31:1–34:12)

### What is the book of Deuteronomy about?

In the book of Deuteronomy, Moses repeats the laws of the covenant that God made with the people of Israel. The people of Israel are about to go into the land that Yahweh had promised them. Before they enter the land, Moses reminds them of what Yahweh did for them and what he expects from them. Moses warns the people about worshiping idols and no longer trusting Yahweh once they settle in the land. Yahweh promises to judge those who disobey him and to bless those who obey his law. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/covenant]])

### How should the title of this book be translated?

The name “Deuteronomy” means “Second Law” or “the retelling of the Law.” Translators may decide on a title such as “A Repeat of the Law” or “Moses Explains the Law Again.” (See: [[rc://*/ta/man/translate/translate-names]])

### Who wrote the book of Deuteronomy?

The writers of both the Old and New Testament present Moses as being very involved with writing the book of Deuteronomy. However, many scholars think that Joshua wrote chapter 34, which tells how Moses died.

### What are the important features of the book of Deuteronomy?

The book contains a series of speeches that Moses gave to Israel before he died. He spoke these things just before the people entered the land that Yahweh had promised them. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/promisedland]])

## Part 2: Important Religious and Cultural Concepts

### Why does Yahweh command the Israelites to completely destroy the Canaanite people who live in the land that Yahweh had promised them?

As Yahweh prepares the Israelites to enter the land that Yahweh had promised them, he commands them to completely destroy the Canaanite people who live there. The Israelites will then not be tempted to join them in worship of their false gods.

## Part 3: Important Translation Issues

### “the place that Yahweh your God will choose to make his name stay,” and “the place that Yahweh your God chooses to put his name” 

The author uses these two phrases, and several other very similar phrases, in Deuteronomy chapters 12, 14, 16, and 26. In them God’s name represents his reputation and presence. These phrases indicate that God would choose a place and make his presence and reputation stay there. That place would be the future temple. (See: [[rc://*/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

### Can this book be translated before the rest of the Pentateuch?

The books of Genesis and Exodus help to explain what happens in Deuteronomy. For this reason, those books should be translated before the book of Deuteronomy.

### One direct quotation inside another

Since this book consists of Moses’ speeches, many parts of this book are direct quotations. Within his speeches, Moses directly quotes what others said. If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate or format these passages so that there are not quotations within a quotation. (See [[rc://*/ta/man/translate/figs-quotesinquotes]])

### Introducing direct quotations

The author of Deuteronomy often uses the word “saying” or “said” to introduce direct quotations even when there is another word describing speaking or commanding. Some languages do not use a word like this. Consider natural ways of introducing direct quotations in your language. (See [[rc://*/ta/man/translate/writing-quotations]])

### Speaking about a future event using the past tense

In Deuteronomy Moses and and Yahweh often speak of a future event using the past tense. For example, speaking of the land that Yahweh had promised them, Yahweh tells the Israelites in 1:8 “I have given the land to” you. In 1:21 Moses tells the Israelites “Yahweh your God has given the land to” you. At the time Yahweh and Moses said these things to the Israelites they had not yet occupied the land that Yahweh had promised them. Moses and Yahweh are using the past tense in order to refer to something that will happen in the future. They are doing this to show that the event will certainly happen. Another example is 2:24, where Moses quotes Yahweh words “I have given into your hand Sihon the Amorite, king of Heshbon, and his land.” Yahweh is using the past tense to emphasize that, in the future, he will certainly enable the Israelites to conquer Sihon and his land. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use the future tense, instead of the past tense, in these three passages and in the other passages in Deuteronomy where the past tense is used to refer to a future event.
(See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/promisedland]] and [[rc://*/ta/man/translate/translate-tense]])

### Yahweh your God, my God, our God

Throughout this book, Moses refers to Yahweh with possessive forms such as “your God,“ “my God,“ and “our God” when he speaks to the Israelites. By using these possessive forms, Moses is not saying that the Israelites possess or control Yahweh. Rather Moses is using these words to indicate that Yahweh is the God whom the Israelites worship. Also, when Moses says, “your God,” he is referring to the same God that he also worships. He is not distinguishing between the God of the Israelites and his own God. (See [[rc://*/ta/man/translate/figs-possession]])

### Moses’ audience

In his speeches, Moses speaks to the Israelites who will enter into the land that Yahweh promised to give to them. Moses reminds them about events that happened to their ancestors and to them. If it would be helpful for your readers, you could state explicitly that Moses is talking about their ancestors even when he directly addresses the living Israelites as “you.” (See [[rc://*/ta/man/translate/writing-pronouns]])

### “you” and “your” singular and plural

Although Moses is speaking to all the Israelites, he sometimes addresses them as “you” singular. Moses wants each of the individual Israelites to think about what he is saying. If it would not be natural in your language to address a group with a singular pronoun, you can use the plural “you” when Moses is speaking to all the Israelites. (See [[rc://*/ta/man/translate/writing-pronouns]] and [[rc://*/ta/man/translate/figs-youcrowd]])

### “to the face of”

Often the author or character use the expression “to the face of” to mean “before,” “in front of,” or “in the presence of” a person or thing. This is by association with the way one can see the face of a person who is present and the way people typically face forward, toward what is before or in front of them. (See: [[rc://*/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

### “in the eyes of,” “eyes of” 

The author and characters often use the term “eyes” by association to mean sight; sight, in turn, represents attention, perspective, and estimation or judgment. For example, Moses speaks of the Israelites doing “evil in the eyes of Yahweh” in 4:25, meaning doing what Yahweh considered wrong and had said was wrong. (See: [[rc://*/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

### “seed”

12 times in Deuteronomy the term **seed** is used with the meaning “offspring” or “descendants.” This use is a word picture. Just as plants produce seeds that grow into more plants, so people can have offspring. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent metaphor from your culture. Alternatively, you could express the meaning plainly. (In Deuteronomy all uses of the word “seed” refer to descendants except 11:10, 14:22, 22:9, and 28:38, where this term refers to literal seed that is planted in the ground.) (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/seed]] and [[rc://*/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

### “listen” 

In this book the term “listen” normally, but not always, means complying with what someone has said. When humans “listen” in this sense, the term means “obey,” as when the Moses says to the Israelites in 1:43 “I spoke to you, but you did not listen.” Moses means, “I spoke to you what Yahweh had commanded me to tell you, but you did not obey.” When Yahweh “listens” in this sense, it means that he does what someone asks in prayer. For example, when Moses says regarding his prayer to Yahweh in 4:25 in which he requested that Yahweh let him cross the Jordan and see the land that Yahweh had promised them, Moses says “But Yahweh was angry with me because of you, and he did not listen to me.” Moses means that Yahweh was angry with him and did not comply with his request to enter land. (See: [[rc://*/ta/man/translate/figs-explicit]])

### “voice”

In this book the word “voice” is often used by association to mean what God or a person said by using their voice. For example, in 8:20 Moses said to the Israelites, “because you would not listen to the voice of Yahweh your God” by which he meant “because you would not listen to what Yahweh your God said to you” or “because you would not listen to the commands that Yahweh your God gave you.” (See: [[rc://*/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

### “go up,” “went up,” “went down,” “brought down” 

In Hebrew, writers and speakers generally indicated whether people were going up to a higher elevation or going down to a lower elevation when they traveled. For example, in 34:1 the author records that “Moses went up from the plains of Moab to Mount Nebo.” In 1:41, the Israelites say “We ourselves shall go up and fight” by which they mean “We ourselves shall go up to the hill country to fight.” If your language does not mark travel for change in elevation, you can translate instances such as these simply as “go” or “went” instead of “go up” or “went up” or “went down.” 

### “to this day”

The author used this phrase to refer to the time when he was writing. The translator should be aware that “to this day” refers to a time that is now in the past. He must avoid giving the impression to his readers that “to this day” means “to the present day.” The translator might decide to use an equivalent phrase such as “at the time of this writing.” This phrase occurs in 2:22, 3:14, 10:8, 11:4, and 29:4, and 34:6. (See: [[rc://*/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

# Deuteronomy 1 Chapter Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter forms a continuation with the last chapter of the book of Numbers. In this chapter is Moses’ first speech to the Israelites.

1. The author’s introduction of Moses’ speech (1–5)
2. Moses reminds the Israelites of Yahweh’s instructions at Mount Horeb to leave Mount Horeb and begin possessing the land that Yahweh had promised them (6-8)
3. Moses chooses judges and military leaders (9-18)
4. Moses recounts the Israelites leaving Mount Horeb and traveling through the wilderness and coming to the hill country of the Amorites and sending out spies to survey the land (19-25)
5. The Israelites unbelief and fear (26-28)
6. Moses’ encourages the Israelites and they persist in their unbelief (29-33)
7. Yahweh’s response (34-40)
8. The response of the Israelites (41-45)
9. Moses’ summary statement (46)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Possessing the land

Moses reminds the Israelites of Yahweh’s command at Mount Horeb to enter and possess the land that Yahweh had promised them. He reminds the Israelites that Yahweh promised he would give them the land of Canaan if they obeyed him. Other people lived in the land, but Yahweh promised to give the Israelites victory over them. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/faithful]] and [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/promisedland]])

### One direct quotation inside another

In this chapter, Moses gives a speech in which he quotes what others have said. If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate or format this passage so that there are no quotations within quotations. (See [[rc://*/ta/man/translate/figs-quotesinquotes]])

# Deuteronomy 2 Chapter Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter continues Moses’ first speech from the previous chapter.

1. Moses recounts the Israelites’ time in the wilderness (1-23)
2. Moses recounts how Yahweh helped the Israelites defeat King Sihon (24-37)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Possessing the land

Yahweh promised the Israelites that he would give them the land of Canaan if they obeyed him. Other people groups lived in the land, but Yahweh promised to give the Israelites victory over them. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/faithful]] and [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/promisedland]])

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### One direct quotation inside another

In this chapter, Moses gives a speech and quotes what others said. If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate or format this passage so that there are no quotations within a quotation. (See [[rc://*/ta/man/translate/figs-quotesinquotes]])

### Moses represents the Israelites

The singular pronoun “you” occurs when Yahweh speaks directly to Moses. The Israelites request that Moses speak to Yahweh on their behalf because the Israelites fear Yahweh and do not want to speak directly to him. Moses acts as a representative on behalf of all the Israelites. If it would be helpful for your readers, you could clarify that Yahweh wants Moses to tell the Israelites everything that Yahweh says.

### Background information

The writer of Deuteronomy adds background information to help readers understand the historical context of Moses’ speech. In the ULT, this information is enclosed in parentheses. Use a method that is natural in your language for indicating that a section of text is background information. (See: [[rc://*/ta/man/translate/writing-background]])

### “you” and “your” singular and plural

The pronouns “you” and “your” are plural in this chapter unless otherwise noted. In those places, although Moses is speaking to all the Israelites, he addresses them as “you” singular. If addressing the Israelites with singular forms would not be natural in your language, you could use plural forms in your translation. (See [[rc://*/ta/man/translate/figs-youcrowd]])
See how you translated the phrase **many days** in [1:46](../01/46.md). Alternate translation: [a very long time]

# Deuteronomy 3 Chapter Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter continues Moses’ speech that began in Chapter 1.

1. Moses recounts how the Israelites defeated King Og and took land east of the Jordan River (1-11)
2. Moses allots land east of the Jordan River to Reuben, Gad, and Manasseh (12-20)
3. Yahweh forbids Moses from entering the land (21-29)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Possessing the land

Yahweh promised the Israelites that he will give them the land of Canaan if they obey him. Other people groups live in the land, but Yahweh promises to give the Israelites victory over them. The land belongs to Israel, but they have not yet entered it to possess the land. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/faithful]] and [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/promisedland]]

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### One direct quotation inside another

In this chapter, Moses gives a speech and quotes what others said. If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate or format this passage so that there are no quotations within a quotation. (See [[rc://*/ta/man/translate/figs-quotesinquotes]])

### Time background

In his speech, Moses reminds the Israelites about what happened to their ancestors before they entered the land that Yahweh promised to give to them. Throughout his speech, Moses repeats the phrase “at that time” to refer to events that occurred during that time period. If it would be helpful for your readers, you could state this information explicitly. (See: [[rc://*/ta/man/translate/writing-newevents]])

# Deuteronomy 4 Chapter Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

1. Moses encourages the Israelites to obey Yahweh (1-40)
2. Cities of refuge selected for the Reubenites, Gadites, and Manassites (41–43)
3. Moses’ introduction of the Law (44-49)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Moses’ instructions

God will not allow Moses to enter into the land he had promised to Israel. Since the Israelites are getting ready to possess the land, Moses gives them some last instructions before his death. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/promisedland]])

### Cities of refuge

Verses 41-43 discuss cities of refuge, which are towns to which a manslayer could flee. In this case, a manslayer is anyone who accidentally kills another person. A close family member of the deceased would be obligated to take revenge for the killing of his family member by finding and killing the person who killed their family member. Yahweh provides protection for the manslayer so that they will not be punished too harshly.
(See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/other/refuge]] and [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/other/avenge]])

### Likeness

Verses 15-31 warn the Israelites against creating idols. The other people groups in the land worshiped entities in nature such as the sun, moon, stars, trees, and so on. They created idols that looked like (in the likeness of) these entities. Yahweh forbids the Israelites from making likenesses of anything for the purpose of worshiping it. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/other/likeness]] and [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/falsegod]])

# Deuteronomy 5 Chapter Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter begins Moses’ second speech to the Israelites and includes the Ten Commandments (6-21).

Some translations set Yahweh’s introductory words in 5:6 and each of the commandments in the list of Ten Commandments in 5:7–21 farther to the right on the page than the rest of the text. The ULT uses a separate paragraph for each commandment.

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Ten Commandments

This chapter repeats the words from Exodus 20, which are known as the Ten Commandments. It is important for the Israelites to obey these words as part of their covenant with Yahweh. Yahweh gave the Israelites the Ten Commandments on Mount Sinai after the Israelites left Egypt. The Ten Commandments were written on two stone tablets that were placed in the ark of the covenant. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/other/tencommandments]] and [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/arkofthecovenant]])

### The Sabbath

Yahweh commands the Israelites to rest on the seventh day, known as the Sabbath. The rest reminds the Israelites that Yahweh rested on the seventh day of creation. The Sabbath also reminds the Israelites that they have rest because Yahweh rescued them from being slaves in Egypt, where they had no rest. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/sabbath]])

Throughout this chapter, when Moses is speaking to the Israelites, he uses the plural forms of “you.” However, in verses 6-21, Yahweh is speaking to Moses and uses singular pronouns.

# Deuteronomy 6 Chapter Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter continues Moses’ second speech, which began in chapter five.

1. The greatest commandment (1-9)
2. A warning against disobeying Yahweh (10-19)
3. Teaching children about Yahweh’s commands (20-25)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Yahweh’s blessings
Yahweh’s continued blessing of the people of Israel is dependent upon the people’s obedience to the law of Moses. When the Israelites agreed to the covenant with Yahweh, they acknowledged that worshiping and obeying Yahweh would lead to blessings, while disobeying him and worshiping other gods would lead to curses. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/bless]] and [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/lawofmoses]])

### The Shema
Verses 6-9 are known as “the Shema” in Judaism. They are an important foundation of Judaism. In [Mark 12:28-29](../../mrk/12/28.md), Jesus identifies the Shema as the greatest commandment.

### Writing Yahweh’s words on one’s arms, forehead, and doorposts

Verses 8-9 command the Israelites always to remember Yahweh’s words. There are different understandings of these commands. Some Jewish traditions interpret these verses as meaning the Israelites should physically write copies of the law. Others believe that the command is to memorize and cherish the law. Translators should be careful to translate the passage as it is, without favoring one interpretation or the other in their translation.

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Words for the law
  - statutes
  - ordinances
  - judgments
Moses uses three different words to refer to the law that Yahweh commanded the Israelites to obey. It is unclear what distinguishes each of these terms from the others. If your language has several terms for the law, you could use them here to differentiate between the various Hebrew words. (See: [[rc://*/ta/man/translate/translate-unknown]])

### “you” and “your” singular and plural

The pronouns “you” and “your” are plural in this chapter unless otherwise noted. Although Moses is speaking to all the Israelites, he sometimes addresses them as “you” singular. If the singular forms of these pronouns would not be natural in your language, you could use the plural forms in your translation. (See [[rc://*/ta/man/translate/figs-youcrowd]])
See how you translated these terms for the law in [5:31](../05/31.md).

# Deuteronomy 7 Chapter Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter continues Moses’ second speech, which began in chapter five.

1. Moses tells the Israelites what they are to do to the seven nations occupying the land that Yahweh had promised them and to those nations' objects of worship (1-11)
2. Blessings for obedience (12-24)
3. Commands regarding what the Israelites are to do with the idols of the false gods of the nations they dispossess (25-26)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### “You must completely destroy them”

The people of Canaan worshiped idols and did other things that were abominations to Yahweh. Since the Israelites had a special relationship with Yahweh, Yahweh used Israel to punish these nations for their idolatry by destroying them completely. Yahweh wanted the Israelites to live differently than those nations. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/sin]] and [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/mercy]])

### Abrahamic Covenant

This chapter references parts of the covenant Yahweh made with Abraham. Yahweh promised Abraham that he would have very many descendants. The Israelites are the descendants of Abraham, so Yahweh repeats his promise to them in Deuteronomy, telling them that they will prosper and increase their population if they obey him. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/covenant]] and [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/faithful]])

# Deuteronomy 8 Chapter Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter continues Moses’ second speech, which began in chapter five. Moses commands the Israelites not to forget Yahweh their God and tells them what will happen if they do (1-20).

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Forgetting

Moses reminds the living Israelites about all the miracles that Yahweh did for them to bring them out of Egypt and survive in the wilderness. In the wilderness, the Israelites complained and grumbled. It was easy for them to forget what Yahweh did for them and disobey Yahweh. As a result, Yahweh punished that generation by causing them to die in the wilderness without entering the land. The living Israelites are the children of that generation. Moses is warning them not to make the same mistakes as their parents did. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/Israel]])

# Deuteronomy 9 Chapter Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter continues Moses’ second speech, which began in chapter five.

1. Moses tells the Israelites that when they enter the land that Yahweh had promised to them that Yahweh will be with them and fight for them (1-3)
2. Moses reminds the Israelites that Yahweh is not allowing them to dispossess the people groups in the land that Yahweh had promised them because of the Israelites righteousness but rather because of the wickedness of the people who live in that land (4-6)
3. Moses recounts the Israelites’ consistent pattern of sinning against Yahweh and his intercession on their behalf (7-29)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Yahweh’s victory
This chapter assures the Israelites that it is Yahweh who will empower them to conquer the land that Yahweh had promised them. The Israelites will not be strong enough on their own to conquer these other nations. This victory will be Yahweh’s. The people did not earn this victory, but it is Yahweh’s punishment of these sinful nations. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/promisedland]] and [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/sin]])

### Israel’s sin
Yahweh is about to punish the Canaanites for their sin. He also reminds Israel of their sin. This serves as a warning to the people of Israel. If they sin again, Yahweh will punish them too.

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### “you”

When Moses is addressing the Israelites, he uses both the singular and plural forms of “you.”

  - In verses 1-6: “you” and “your” are singular.
  - In verse 7 see the note.
  - In verses 8-9 “you” and “your” are plural.
  - In verses 16-25 “you” and “your” are plural.

Although Moses is speaking to all the Israelites, he sometimes addresses them as “you” singular. If the singular forms of these pronouns would not be natural in your language, you could use the plural forms in your translation. (See: [[rc://*/ta/man/translate/writing-pronouns]] and [[rc://*/ta/man/translate/figs-youcrowd]])

# Deuteronomy 10 Chapter Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter continues Moses’ second speech, which began in chapter five.

1. Yahweh writes the commandments on stone tablets again (1-5)
2. Aaron dies, the priesthood continues, and the special role of the Levites (6-9)
3. Yahweh listens to Moses and does not destroy the Israelites (10-11)
4. Moses encourages the Israelites to obey Yahweh (12-22)

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter is a continuation of the previous chapter.

# Deuteronomy 11 Chapter Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter continues Moses’ second speech, which began in chapter five.

1. Moses wants the Israelites to obey Yahweh because of his miracles (1-7)
2. Blessings for obedience (8-15)
3. Warnings for disobedience (16-17)
4. The importance of Yahweh’s words (18-25)
5. Instructions on the blessings and curses (26-32)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Placing Yahweh’s words on one’s arms, forehead, and doorposts

Verses 18-20 command the Israelites to always remember Yahweh’s words. There are different understandings of these commands. Some Jewish traditions interpret these verses as meaning that the Israelites should physically write copies of the law. Others believe that the command is to memorize and cherish the law. Translators should be careful to translate the passage as it is, without implying one interpretation or the other in their translation.

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### “you”

When Moses is addressing the Israelites, he uses both the singular and plural forms of “you.” 

  - In verse 1 “you” and “your” are singular.
  - In verses 2-9 “you” and “your” are plural.
  - In verse 10 see the note.
  - In verses 11-13 “you” and “your” are plural.

# Deuteronomy 12 Chapter Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter continues Moses’ second speech, which began in chapter five.

1. The statutes and the ordinances that Yahweh commands the Israelites to keep in the land that Yahweh had promised them (1-31)
2. Yahweh commands the Israelites not to add or take away from the commands he has given them (32)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Covenant with Moses

This chapter is a continuation of the covenant Yahweh made with Moses. The reasons for these food restrictions are not always known. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/covenant]] and [[rc://*/ta/man/translate/figs-explicit]])

### Israel and Yahweh

In the ancient Near East, when nations conquered other nations, they often added the gods of the conquered nation into the collection of gods they worshiped. It was rare to worship only one God. Israel was to be known for worshiping Yahweh and Yahweh alone. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/falsegod]])

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Words for the law

  - statutes
  - ordinances
  - judgments

Moses uses several words to refer to the law that Yahweh commanded the Israelites to obey. It is unclear what the differences are between these terms. If your language has different terms for the law, you could use them here to differentiate between the different Hebrew words. (See: [[rc://*/ta/man/translate/translate-unknown]])

### “you” and “your” singular and plural

The pronouns “you” and “your” are plural in this chapter unless otherwise noted. Although Moses is speaking to all the Israelites, from verses 13-32 he addresses them as “you” singular. Moses wants each individual to obey the law for themselves. If the singular forms of these pronouns would not be natural in your language, you could use the plural forms in your translation. (See [[rc://*/ta/man/translate/figs-youcrowd]])

### “the place that Yahweh your God will choose”

Moses uses phrases such as this to refer to the future place where the temple will be built. These phrases emphasize that Yahweh will be the one who decides where the Israelites will build his temple as well as how they will worship him. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/temple]])

### “the place Yahweh your God will choose … to put his name,” “the place that Yahweh your God will choose to make his name stay,” “the place that Yahweh your God chooses to put his name”

In 12:5, 12:11 and 12:21 the author uses God’s name to represent his reputation and presence. These phrases indicate that God would choose a place and make his presence and reputation stay there. That place would be the future temple. (See: [[rc://*/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

# Deuteronomy 13 Chapter Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter continues Moses’ second speech, which began in chapter five.

1. Instructions regarding Israelite prophets and dreamers of dreams who try to entice fellow Israelites to worship false gods (1-5)
2. Instructions regarding Israelite family members who try to entice an Israelite family member to worship false gods (6-11)
3. Instructions regarding the worship of false gods in Israelite cities (12-18)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### False prophecy

Verses 1-11 discuss false prophets and people who practice divination. These are people would encourage people to worship idols instead of Yahweh and therefore Yahweh commanded that they must be put to death. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/false-prophet]] and [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/divination]])

### Abominations

Anything that is sinful or ceremonially impure according to the law is called an “abomination” in this chapter. The sinful things include people who worship idols, items used for idol worship, and anything associated with idolatry. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/detest]] and [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/wicked]])

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Hypothetical conditions

Moses is addressing situations that could occur in the future and giving instructions for the Israelites to follow if those situations occur. In your translation, be sure to use phrases that show that Moses is talking about hypothetical situations, not promising that something will happen in the future. (See: [[rc://*/ta/man/translate/grammar-connect-condition-hypothetical]])

# Deuteronomy 14 Chapter Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter continues Moses’ second speech, which began in chapter five.

1. Commands for mourning practices (1-2)
2. Commands regarding the eating of animals (3-21)
3. Commands regarding tithing (22-29)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Law of Moses

This chapter is part of the law of Moses, which is part of the covenant Yahweh made with Moses. Yahweh will enable the Israelites to live on the land if they obey his commands. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/lawofmoses]])

### Clean animals

There are animals which the law considered to be clean and unclean. The people were not allowed to eat the unclean animals. Scholars are not certain about the reasons that some animals are to be considered clean and others unclean. The result of these food restrictions was a nation that was different from the nations surrounding it. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/clean]])

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### “you” and “your” singular and plural

Moses is speaking to all the Israelites, so all forms of the second person pronouns “you” and “your” are plural in this chapter unless otherwise specified. Use the plural form in your translation if your language marks that distinction. (See: [[rc://*/ta/man/translate/figs-yousingular]] and [[rc://*/ta/man/translate/writing-pronouns]]) (See [[rc://*/ta/man/translate/figs-youcrowd]])

### Types of living creatures

This chapter discusses which living creatures are permissible for the Israelites to eat. It is unclear which specific creatures some of the Hebrew terms refer to, but the general categories of these creatures are explained in the notes. Additionally, your readers may not be familiar with many of these creatures. In your translation, you could use broad categories of animals, such as fish, birds of prey, and cattle. Or, you could use the names of creatures in your area that are similar to the ones mentioned in this chapter. (See: [[rc://*/ta/man/translate/translate-unknown]])

### “the place that Yahweh your God will choose”

Moses uses phrases such as this to refer to the future place where the temple will be built. These phrases emphasize that Yahweh will be the one who decides where the Israelites will build his temple as well as how they will worship him. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/temple]])

### “the place that he will choose to make his name stay,” “the place that Yahweh your God will choose to put his name” 

In 14:23 and 14:24 the author uses God’s name to represent his reputation and presence. These phrases indicate that God would choose a place and make his presence and reputation stay there. That place would be the future temple. (See: [[rc://*/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

# Deuteronomy 15 Chapter Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter continues Moses’ second speech, which began in chapter five.

1. Rules for canceling debts (1-11)
2. Rules for fellow Israelite slaves (12-18)
3. Rules for firstborn male animals (19-23)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Israelite slaves

This chapter contains rules for owning slaves that were fellow Israelites. An Israelite might work as another Israelite’s slave to pay off a debt. Instead of receiving pay, their wages would go toward their debt. The debtor would be their creditor’s property, and they could not work elsewhere. If the word “slave” would not accurately describe this practice in your culture, you could use a comparable term, such as “indentured servant” or “bondservant.” (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/other/servant]])

# Deuteronomy 16 Chapter Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter continues Moses’ second speech, which began in chapter five.

1. Instructions for the Festival of the Passover (1-8)
2. Instructions for the Festival of the Harvest (9-12)
3. Instructions for the Feast of Huts (13-17)
4. Administration of justice (18-20)
5. Asherah poles and pillars forbidden (21-22)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Feasts

This chapter gives instructions for the feasts that Yahweh commanded the Israelites to celebrate. The Passover feast represents the time when the Israelites escaped from Egypt. There are several other important festivals described in this chapter. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/passover]])

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### “you” and “your” singular

Even though Moses is addressing all the Israelites, he uses the singular forms of “you” and “your.” If the singular forms of these pronouns would not be natural in your language, you could use the plural forms in your translation. (See: [[rc://*/ta/man/translate/figs-youcrowd]])

### “the place that Yahweh will choose”

Moses uses phrases such as this to refer to the future place where the temple will be built. These phrases emphasize that Yahweh will be the one who decides where the Israelites will build his temple as well as how they will worship him. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/temple]])

### “the place that Yahweh will choose to make his name stay”

# Deuteronomy 17 Chapter Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter continues Moses’ second speech, which began in chapter five.

1. More instructions for animals for sacrifice (1)
2. Punishments for Israelites who worship idols (2-7)
3. Instructions for difficult legal cases (8-13)
4. Instructions for kings (14-20)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Witnesses

In the ancient Near East, it was common for a person to be punished by the testimony of a single person, especially if this was an important person. The rules in this chapter give protection to people, especially the poor by requiring multiple witnesses. This allowed justice to be done. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/testimony]] and [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/justice]])

### King

Israel was not to have a king because Yahweh was their king. Knowing the sinfulness of the people, Yahweh anticipated that one day Israel would have a king. Therefore, this passage gives commands about their king prophetically. They were not allowed to collect chariots because they were a sign of earthly power and the king was to trust in Yahweh. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/prophet]], [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/sign]] and [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/trust]])

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### “you” and “your” singular

Even though Moses is addressing all the Israelites, he uses the singular forms of “you.” If the singular forms of these pronouns would not be natural in your language, you could use the plural forms in your translation. (See: [[rc://*/ta/man/translate/figs-youcrowd]])

### Generic nouns used in hypothetical conditions

Verses 2-13 give examples of sins that an Israelite might commit when they are living in the land and instructions for deciding what should happen. In these hypothetical conditions, singular nouns like “man,” “woman,” and “judge” represent those people in general, not a specific man or woman whom Moses is predicting will commit a sin. If it would be helpful in your language, you could clarify that these terms refer to any person who fulfills the hypothetical situation. (See: [[rc://*/ta/man/translate/figs-genericnoun]] and [[rc://*/ta/man/translate/grammar-connect-condition-hypothetical]])

# Deuteronomy 18 Chapter Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter continues Moses’ second speech, which began in chapter five.

1. Yahweh’s provision for the priests and all Levites (1-8)
2. Warnings against pagan religious practices (9-14)
3. Yahweh promises to send a prophet like Moses (15-22)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Levites

As Yahweh’s chosen priests, the Levites were to trust in Yahweh to provide for them. They did not inherit any land, but Yahweh was their inheritance, in the sense that they received the privilege of being his priests. Yahweh provided for their needs through the rest of the Israelites, because the Levites were allowed to eat portions of the sacrifices that the Israelites sacrificed to Yahweh. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/elect]], [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/priest]] and [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/trust]] and [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/inherit]])

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### “you” and “your” singular

Even though Moses is addressing all the Israelites, he uses the singular forms of “you.” If the singular forms of these pronouns would not be natural in your language, you could use the plural forms in your translation. (See: [[rc://*/ta/man/translate/figs-youcrowd]])

### Generic nouns in hypothetical situations

Verses 6-10 and 20-22 give instructions and warnings for the Israelites. In these hypothetical conditions, singular nouns like “Levite,” “maker,” and “prophet” represent those groups of people in general, not a specific person. If it would be helpful in your language, you could clarify that these terms refer to any person who fulfills the hypothetical situation. (See: [[rc://*/ta/man/translate/figs-genericnoun]] and [[rc://*/ta/man/translate/grammar-connect-condition-hypothetical]])

# Deuteronomy 19 Chapter Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter continues Moses’ second speech, which began in chapter five.

1. Cities of refuge (1-13)
2. Property lines (14)
3. Rules regarding witnesses (15-21)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Witnesses

In the ancient Near East, it was common for a person to be punished by the testimony of a single person, especially if this was an important person. The rules in this chapter give protection to people, especially the poor, by requiring multiple witnesses. This allowed justice to be done. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/testimony]])

### Cities of refuge

Verses 1-13 discuss cities of refuge, which are towns to which a killer could flee. These verses address both cases where the killer accidentally kills another person and cases where the killer plans the murder. In those times, a close family member of the deceased would be obligated to take revenge for the killing of his family member by finding and killing the manslayer (someone who accidentally kills another human being). Yahweh provides protection for the killer who killed accidentally so that he will not be punished too harshly.
(See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/other/refuge]] and [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/other/avenge]])

# Deuteronomy 20 Chapter Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter continues Moses’ second speech, which began in chapter five.

1. Instructions for going to war (20:1-20)
2. Encouragement and exemptions from battle (20:1-9)
3. Rules for sieges and warfare (20:10-20)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Yahweh’s protection in battle

Israel was not to fear the military might of other nations. Their confidence was to be in Yahweh, who was the true source of their strength and protection. This divine reliance is highlighted by the priest, rather than a military commander, addressing the soldiers before battle, reminding them of Yahweh’s presence and power to save them. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/trust]] and [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/priest]])

### Holy war and the conquest of Canaan

The conquest of the land that Yahweh had promised them was a unique event in Israel’s history, considered a form of holy war with specific, God-given rules. This warfare was presented as Yahweh’s judgment against the sinfulness of the Canaanite peoples. The command for complete destruction of these peoples was to prevent them from leading Israel into sin. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/promisedland]] and [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/holy]] and [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/sin]])

### Exemptions from military service

In ancient Israelite society, certain men were excused from military service. This chapter outlines several reasons for exemption, including recently building a new house, planting a new vineyard and not yet enjoying its fruit, being newly engaged to a woman, or being fearful. These exemptions ensured that important life events were honored and that the army consisted of willing and courageous soldiers.

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Use of “you”

Throughout this chapter, Moses is addressing the entire nation of Israel.
  * **Singular “you” addressing the crowd:** Most often, Moses uses the singular form of “you” (e.g., 20:1 “When **you** go out … **you** shall not fear,” 20:10 “When **you** draw near … **you** shall call”). This is a common Hebrew rhetorical device where the community is addressed as a single entity.
  * **Plural “you”:** The priest, when addressing the people in 20:3-4, uses the plural form of “you” (e.g., 20:3 “your hearts,” “of them,” 20:4 “your God,” “with you,” “for you,” “your enemies,” “save you”). The officers also use plural forms when they address the people (e.g., 20:18 “teach you”).
If addressing a crowd with a singular “you” is unnatural in your language, consistently use the plural form.

### “what man is there”

This phrase, used multiple times in verses 5-8 (e.g., “Who is the man that has built a new house”), introduces rhetorical questions. These questions are not seeking information but are designed to identify categories of men who are to be excused from battle, emphasizing Yahweh’s desire for a dedicated fighting force. (See: [[rc://*/ta/man/translate/figs-rquestion]])

### “soften your hearts” / “heart … will not melt”

In 20:3, “You shall not soften your hearts” is an idiom meaning “do not be afraid.” Similarly, in 20:8, the phrase “the heart of his brother will not melt like his heart” means his fellow soldiers will not become afraid like he is. The heart here represents courage. If these idioms are not clear, translate them with their plain meaning. (See: [[rc://*/ta/man/translate/figs-idiom]] and [[rc://*/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

### “mouth of the sword”

The expression “by the mouth of the sword” in 20:13 is an idiom meaning to kill with a sword, often implying complete destruction in battle. Translate this with a natural equivalent in your language. (See: [[rc://*/ta/man/translate/figs-idiom]])

### “For is the tree of the field a man?”

This rhetorical question in 20:19 emphasizes that trees are not enemies to be attacked during a siege. It implies that since trees are not human combatants, they should not be indiscriminately destroyed, especially if they provide food. (See: [[rc://*/ta/man/translate/figs-rquestion]] and [[rc://*/ta/man/translate/figs-personification]])

# Deuteronomy 21 Chapter Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter continues Moses’ second speech, which began in chapter five.

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Atonement for unsolved murder

Verses 1-9 outline a specific ritual for atoning for a murder when the killer is unknown. This involved the elders of the nearest town, a heifer that had never worked, and a valley with running water that had not been cultivated. Breaking the heifer’s neck was a symbolic act to cleanse the land and the community from the guilt of the shed blood, demonstrating the seriousness with which unexplained deaths were treated and the need for communal responsibility. (See: [[rc://*/ta/man/translate/translate-symaction]])

### Treatment of female captives of war

Verses 10-14 provide instructions for an Israelite man who wishes to marry a woman taken captive in war. She was to be given a month to mourn her parents, shave her head, and trim her nails. These actions symbolized her transition from her old life and her grief. If the man later decided he did not want her, he had to let her go free and could not sell her, recognizing the humiliation she had already endured.

### Rights of the firstborn son

Verses 15-17 address the inheritance rights of the firstborn son, even if he was the son of a less-loved wife. The firstborn was entitled to a double portion of the father’s estate, and this right could not be transferred to the son of a more favored wife. This upheld the principle of justice and the accepted customs about how the oldest son inherited things.

### Dealing with a rebellious son

Verses 18-21 describe a judicial process for a persistently rebellious son who disobeys his parents despite discipline. Such a son was to be brought before the elders at the city gate and, if found guilty, stoned to death by the men of the city. This severe punishment was to remove “the evil” from the community and serve as a deterrent.

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Use of “you”

Throughout this chapter, Moses is addressing the entire nation of Israel.
  * **Singular “you” addressing the crowd:** Moses consistently uses the singular form of “you” when giving these laws (e.g., 21:1 “Yahweh **your** God is giving to **you**,” 21:9 “**you** shall remove … when **you** do,” 21:10 “When **you** go out … Yahweh **your** God … **your** hand … **you** take,” 21:23 “**your** land … Yahweh **your** God is giving to **you**“).
  * **Exception – plural “you” in address by elders:** The elders, in their prescribed speech in 21:7, use plural forms when referring to themselves (“Our hands … our eyes”).
If addressing a crowd with a singular “you” is unnatural in your language, consistently use the plural form for Moses‘ address.

### “elders and your judges”

In 21:2, the terms “your elders and your judges” refer to distinct but related leadership roles. Elders were respected older men involved in local governance, while judges had a more formal role in adjudicating legal cases. If these specific roles are not familiar, use terms for similar leadership positions in your culture or a descriptive phrase. (See: [[rc://*/ta/man/translate/translate-unknown]])

### “Cover, Yahweh, your people Israel”

In 21:8, the elders pray, “Cover, Yahweh, your people Israel.” The word “Cover” is a metaphor asking Yahweh to forgive and protect his people from the guilt of the unsolved murder. 

### “beginning of his strength”

The phrase “he is the beginning of his strength” in 21:17, referring to the firstborn son, is a metaphor for the father’s first demonstration of his ability to produce offspring.

# Deuteronomy 22 Chapter Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter continues Moses’ second speech, which began in chapter five.

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Maintaining order and integrity

Many laws in this chapter aim to maintain order, compassion, and integrity within the Israelite community. These include returning lost property (22:1-3), helping a fallen animal (22:4), preserving distinct gender roles in dress (22:5), showing compassion to mother birds (22:6-7), ensuring safety in home construction (22:8), and avoiding prohibited mixtures in agriculture and clothing (22:9-11). These laws reflect Yahweh’s concern for justice, kindness, and holiness in everyday life.

### Purity and separation

The prohibitions against mixing seeds in a vineyard (22:9), plowing with an ox and a donkey together (22:10), and wearing clothing woven of wool and linen together (22:11) symbolize the importance of maintaining distinctions and purity. These laws served as tangible reminders for Israel to remain a people set apart for Yahweh, distinct from surrounding nations and their practices.

### Marital purity and justice in accusations

A significant portion of the chapter (22:13-29) deals with issues of marital purity, accusations of premarital sex, adultery, and rape. The laws provide procedures for verifying a bride’s virginity if questioned and prescribe severe penalties for false accusations, adultery, and sexual violence. These laws aimed to protect the integrity of marriage, ensure justice, and remove evil from the community. The requirement for a bloodstained cloth as proof of virginity (22:15-17) was a specific cultural practice.

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Use of “you”

Throughout this chapter, Moses is addressing the entire nation of Israel.
  * **Singular “you” addressing the crowd:** Moses consistently uses the singular form of “you” when giving these laws (e.g., 22:1 “When **you** see … **your** brother … **you** shall not hide **yourself** … **you** shall return them to **your** brother,” 22:8 “When **you** build … **your** roof … **you** will not bring … in **your** house,” 22:12 “**you** shall make … for **yourself** … **your** garment … **you** cover **yourself**“).
  * **Plural “you”:** When addressing the community regarding the execution of offenders or bringing them to the gate, plural forms are used for “you” (e.g., 22:21 “they shall bring **out** the girl … the men of **her** city shall stone **her** … and **you** shall remove the evil,” 22:24 “then **you** shall take both of them … and stone **them** … and **you** shall remove the evil”).
If addressing a crowd with a singular “you” is unnatural in your language, consistently use the plural form for Moses‘ address, but ensure the switch to plural for communal actions is clear.

### “hide yourself from them”

In 22:1, 3, and 4, the phrase “and hide yourself from them” is a metaphor for deliberately ignoring a situation that requires action or avoiding responsibility (e.g., a lost animal or a fallen animal). (See: [[rc://*/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

### Repetition for emphasis (reduplication)

Moses uses repetition of verb forms for emphasis in several commands:
  *   22:1: “returning, you shall return them” (הָשֵׁ֥ב תְּשִׁיבֵ֖⁠ם) emphasizes the certainty of returning the lost animal.
  *   22:4: “lifting, you shall lift it up” (הָקֵ֥ם תָּקִ֖ים) emphasizes the certainty of helping the fallen animal.
  *   22:7: “Sending, you shall send away” (שַׁלֵּ֤חַ תְּשַׁלַּח֙) emphasizes the absolute requirement to release the mother bird.
If your language uses repetition for emphasis, you may replicate this. Otherwise, use another natural way to express strong obligation, such as “you must certainly …” or “you absolutely must …” (See: [[rc://*/ta/man/translate/figs-reduplication]])

### Euphemisms for sexual relations

This chapter uses several euphemisms for sexual intercourse:
  *   22:13: “he goes in to her” 
  *   22:14: “I came near to her” 
  *   22:22, 23, 25, 28: “lying with” / “lies with her”
Translate these with polite and culturally appropriate expressions in your language, or state the meaning plainly if euphemisms would be obscure. (See: [[rc://*/ta/man/translate/figs-euphemism]])

### “uncover the hem of his father”

The idiom in 22:30, “he shall not uncover the hem of his father,” means to have sexual relations with his father’s wife, thereby violating his father’s marriage and honor. If this idiom is not clear, translate it with its plain meaning. (See: [[rc://*/ta/man/translate/figs-idiom]])

# Deuteronomy 23 Chapter Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter continues Moses’ second speech, which began in chapter five.

1. Exclusions from the assembly of Yahweh (1-8)
    1. Those with physical defects (1)
    2. Those of illegitimate birth (2)
    3. Ammonites and Moabites (3-6)
    4. Edomites and Egyptians (7-8)
2. Maintaining holiness in the military camp (9-14)
3. Various laws concerning social and religious conduct (15-25)
    1. Protecting escaped slaves (15-16)
    2. Prohibition of cultic prostitution (17-18)
    3. Laws on charging interest (19-20)
    4. Fulfilling vows (21-23)
    5. Gleaning from a neighbor’s field (24-25)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### The assembly of Yahweh

The phrase “assembly of Yahweh” (or “Yahweh’s people” in the simplified text) appears multiple times at the beginning of this chapter (1, 2, 3, 8). This term refers to the formal, convened community of Israel, particularly when gathered for religious worship, legal decisions, or important communal matters. Exclusion from this assembly meant being barred from full participation in these central aspects of Israelite life and worship. The reasons for exclusion outlined in this chapter relate to physical wholeness (reflecting the holiness required in Yahweh’s presence), lineage (due to past hostilities or illegitimate birth, which could carry social and religious stigma), and historical relationships with other nations. These rules emphasized the holiness and separateness of Yahweh’s people.

### Maintaining holiness and purity

Several laws in this chapter are concerned with maintaining holiness and purity, both within the community generally and specifically within the military camp. The exclusion of certain individuals from the assembly (1-8) and the detailed instructions for camp sanitation (9-14) highlight the idea that Yahweh’s presence required a clean and set-apart environment. Uncleanness, whether physical or ritual, was incompatible with the presence of a holy God.

### Treatment of foreigners and vulnerable people

The chapter includes laws concerning the treatment of escaped slaves (15-16), prohibiting their return to their masters and ensuring their protection. It also distinguishes between charging interest to fellow Israelites (forbidden) and foreigners (permitted) (19-20). 

### Cultic prostitution and vows

The strong prohibition against cultic prostitution (17-18), both male and female, and the refusal to accept money earned from such practices for vows, underscores Yahweh’s rejection of Canaanite religious practices, which often involved sexual rituals. The laws regarding vows (21-23) emphasize the seriousness of making a promise to Yahweh and the obligation to fulfill it.

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Use of “you”

Moses primarily addresses the entire nation of Israel using the singular form of “you” throughout this chapter.
  * **Singular “you” addressing the crowd:** This is the consistent pattern when Moses is delivering the laws (e.g., 23:4 “when **you** had come out,” 23:5 “Yahweh **your** God … blessing for **you**,” 23:9 “When **you** go out … **you** shall keep,” 23:19 “**You** shall not charge interest to **your** brother,” 23:21 “When **you** vow … Yahweh **your** God … for **you**”).
  * **Plural “you” in specific address:** When Moses refers to the Israelites’ past experience in 23:4, “they did not meet **you** [plural] with bread and with water … they hired against **you** [plural] Balaam … to curse **you** [plural].” the plural is used to refer to the people at that historical moment. The direct address to the current generation then generally resumes with the singular.

If addressing the community with a singular “you” is unnatural in your language, use the plural form for Moses’ direct address to the current generation.

### “no man may take a mill or an upper millstone as a pledge”

A millstone was the way a person made a living. To take a person’s millstone was to take away the way they earned money and produced food. (See: [[rc://*/ta/man/translate/figs-explicit]])

### Lending money

Lending money to fellow Israelites was a way to help them out. It was not intended to be a way to make money off their brothers. This chapter gives limitations regarding the lending of money.
